rounds.proof_sketch: Fixed input shape [16, 16384] → size = 16 × 16384 = 262,144 elements. Original threshold: 262144 >= 1024 → TRUE (vectorized). Mutated threshold: 262144 >= 1025 → TRUE (vectorized). Both conditions evaluate identically for any size > 1024. The mutation would only be observable when size == 1024, which requires changing the input shape.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes the host-side threshold from 1024 to 1025 that determines which kernel (vectorized vs scalar) to launch. With the fixed input shape [16, 16384] containing 262,144 elements, this size vastly exceeds both thresholds. Both the original condition `size >= 1024` and the mutated condition `size >= 1025` evaluate to TRUE for 262,144 elements, causing both versions to always execute the identical vectorized kernel. The threshold check depends solely on tensor size (element count), not on tensor values. No value-level variation can change the tensor's element count, making this mutation impossible to distinguish without modifying the input shape to have exactly 1024 elements.
rounds.kill_strategy: This mutant is unkillable under the fixed-shape contract. The mutation affects only the threshold for kernel selection (1024 vs 1025), and the fixed input size of 262,144 elements is far above both thresholds. To kill this mutant would require an input tensor with exactly 1024 elements, which violates the fixed-shape constraint of [16, 16384].
rounds.recommendations: When testing threshold-based kernel selection mutations, the test framework should include tensor sizes at exact boundary values (e.g., 1024, 1025 elements) to exercise both branches of the kernel selection logic. For fixed-shape contracts where this isn't possible, such threshold mutations should be flagged as configuration-dependent and tested through a separate configuration-stress track with appropriate input sizes.
